final_text: I walked for a while on the paved path; but a subtle, familiar scent—cigar smoke—drifted from a window. I saw the library casement open a few inches; I knew I might be watched from there, so I went apart into the orchard. No corner of the grounds was more sheltered or more like Eden: it was full of trees and blooming with flowers. A very high wall shut it off from the courtyard on one side; on the other, a beech avenue screened it from the lawn. At the far end was a sunken fence—its only boundary with the open fields beyond. A winding path bordered with laurels and ending at a giant horse-chestnut tree, ringed at the base by a bench, led down to the fence. Here one could wander unseen. While such sweet dew fell, such silence reigned, such twilight gathered, I felt as if I could haunt this shade forever. But as I threaded the flower and fruit beds at the upper end of the enclosure, drawn there by the light the now-rising moon cast on this more open area, my step was checked—not by any sound or sight, but once again by a warning fragrance.

final_text: It is one of my flaws that though my tongue can sometimes produce a ready answer, there are times when it fails me badly in framing an excuse—and always at some crisis, when a smooth word or plausible pretext is most needed to save me from painful awkwardness. I did not like walking alone with Mr. Rochester in the shadowy orchard at this hour; but I could not think of a reason to leave him. I followed with dragging steps, my thoughts busy searching for an escape. But he himself looked so composed and so serious that I grew ashamed of my confusion: the danger—if any existed or was to come—seemed to be entirely in my own mind; his was calm and undisturbed.

final_text: I said this almost involuntarily, and, with as little exercise of free will, my tears broke free. I did not cry loudly, though; I avoided sobbing. The thought of Mrs. O'Gall and Bitternutt Lodge struck cold to my heart; colder still the thought of all the brine and foam destined, it seemed, to rush between me and the master at whose side I now walked; and coldest of all the awareness of the wider ocean—wealth, class, custom—that lay between me and the one I naturally and inevitably loved.

We'll talk over the voyage and the parting quietly for half an hour or so, while the stars come out up in heaven. Here is the chestnut tree: here is the bench at its old roots. Come, we will sit here in peace tonight, though we may never again be destined to sit here together." He sat me down and then sat beside me.

final_text: I could risk no sort of answer now: my heart stood still.

final_text: In listening, I sobbed convulsively; for I could no longer suppress what I was enduring; I had to give way, and I was shaken from head to foot with raw distress. When I did speak, it was only to utter a passionate wish that I had never been born, or never come to Thornfield.

problem: Source 'excluded from every glimpse of communion with what is bright and energetic and high' — modern drops 'communion with', so Jane is shut out from seeing, not from sharing in, such minds.
final_text: "I grieve to leave Thornfield. I love Thornfield—I love it because I have lived here a full and wonderful life, even if only briefly. I have not been trampled on. I have not been turned to stone. I have not been buried among inferior minds, shut out from every glimpse of communion with what is bright and vital and high. I have talked, face to face, with what I revere, with what I delight in—with an original, a powerful, an expansive mind. I have known you, Mr. Rochester; and it strikes me with terror and anguish to feel I absolutely must be torn from you forever. I see the necessity of going; and it is like staring at the necessity of death."

final_text: "Am I a liar in your eyes?" he asked passionately. "Little sceptic, you shall be convinced. What love have I for Miss Ingram? None—and you know it. What love has she for me? None—as I have taken care to prove. I made sure a rumour reached her that my fortune was not a third of what people supposed, and then I presented myself to see the result; it was coldness, both from her and her mother. I would not—I could not—marry Miss Ingram. You—you strange, you almost unearthly thing!—I love as my own flesh. You—poor and obscure, and small and plain as you are—I beg you to accept me as a husband."

final_text: "God pardon me!" he added soon after. "And let no one interfere: I have her, and I will hold her."

final_text: "No—that is the best of it," he said. And if I had loved him less, I might have thought his tone and look of triumph savage. But sitting beside him, woken from the nightmare of separation, called to the paradise of union, I thought only of the bliss given me to drink in such abundant measure. Again and again he asked, "Are you happy, Jane?" And again and again I answered, "Yes." After which he murmured, "It will atone—it will atone. Did I not find her friendless, cold, and comfortless? Will I not guard and cherish and comfort her? Is there not love in my heart, and constancy in my resolve? It will make amends before God's tribunal. I know my Maker approves what I do. For the world's judgment—I wash my hands of it. For human opinion—I defy it."

final_text: I was not surprised, when I ran down into the hall, to find that a brilliant June morning had followed the night's storm, and to feel, through the open glass door, the breath of a fresh, fragrant breeze. Nature had to be cheerful when I was so happy. A beggar woman and her little boy — both pale, ragged figures — were coming up the walk. I ran down and gave them all the money I happened to have in my purse, three or four shillings. Deserving or not, they had to share in my celebration. The rooks cawed, and brighter birds sang, but nothing was so merry or so musical as my own rejoicing heart.

final_text: "Jane, you look blooming, and smiling, and pretty," he said. "Truly pretty this morning. Is this my pale little elf? Is this my mustard-seed? This little sunny-faced girl with the dimpled cheek and rosy lips, the satin-smooth hazel hair and the radiant hazel eyes?" (I had green eyes, reader, but you must excuse the mistake. For him they were newly dyed, I suppose.)

final_text: I did, and I could not quite take it in. It made me dizzy. The feeling his announcement sent through me was something stronger than was consistent with joy — something that struck and stunned. It was, I think, almost fear.

final_text: "You shall stay in Paris, Rome, and Naples — in Florence, Venice, and Vienna. All the ground I have wandered over shall be walked again by you. Wherever I stamped my hoof, your sylph's foot shall step also. Ten years ago I flew through Europe half mad, with disgust, hate, and rage as my companions. Now I shall revisit it healed and renewed, with an angel at my side as my comfort."

final_text: "I never met your equal. Jane, you please me and you master me — you seem to submit, and I like the sense of pliancy you give; and while I am winding the soft, silken thread around my finger, it sends a thrill up my arm to my heart. I am influenced — conquered. And the influence is sweeter than I can express, and the conquest I undergo has a witchery beyond any triumph I can win. Why do you smile, Jane? What does that mysterious, uncanny expression mean?"

final_text: "Is it, sir? You give in very quickly. How stern you look now! Your eyebrows have grown as thick as my finger, and your forehead resembles what I once saw described in some very astonishing poetry as 'a blue-piled thunderloft.' That will be your married look, sir, I suppose?"

final_text: I was soon dressed. When I heard Mr. Rochester leave Mrs. Fairfax's parlour, I hurried down to it. The old lady had been reading her morning portion of Scripture — the lesson for the day. Her Bible lay open before her, and her spectacles were upon it. Her reading, interrupted by Mr. Rochester's announcement, seemed now forgotten. Her eyes, fixed on the blank wall opposite, expressed the surprise of a quiet mind stirred by unexpected news. Seeing me, she roused herself, made a sort of effort to smile, and framed a few words of congratulation. But the smile faded, and the sentence was left unfinished. She put away her spectacles, shut the Bible, and pushed her chair back from the table.

final_text: "No, you are perfectly fine, and much improved of late. And Mr. Rochester, I daresay, is fond of you. I have always noticed that you were a sort of favourite of his. There are times when, for your sake, I have been a little uneasy at his obvious preference and have wished to warn you. But I did not like to suggest even the possibility of anything wrong. I knew such an idea would shock, perhaps offend you, and you were so discreet, so thoroughly modest and sensible, that I hoped you could be trusted to look after yourself. Last night I cannot tell you what I suffered when I searched all over the house and could find neither you nor the master anywhere. And then, at midnight, I saw you come in with him."

If you have a taste for anything in that line, away with you, sir, to the bazaars of Istanbul without delay, and spend on extensive slave-purchases some of that spare cash you seem at a loss to use up satisfactorily here."

But listen — I'll whisper. It is your turn now, little tyrant, but mine will come soon. And when once I have fairly seized you, to have and to hold, I'll just — figuratively speaking — attach you to a chain like this" (touching his watch chain). "Yes, bonny wee thing, I'll wear you close to my heart, lest my jewel I should lose."

final_text: He duly summoned me to his presence that evening. I had prepared an occupation for him, for I was determined not to spend the whole time in private conversation. I remembered his fine voice. I knew he liked to sing — good singers generally do. I was no vocalist myself and, in his exacting judgment, no musician either, but I loved listening when the performance was good. No sooner had twilight, that hour of romance, begun to lower her blue and starry banner over the window than I rose, opened the piano, and begged him, for the love of heaven, to give me a song. He said I was a fickle witch and that he would rather sing another time, but I insisted that no time was like the present.
